rows.question: i have [[Hardened Scales]] and [[Doubling Season]] and cast ballista for X=2. how many counters does it come in with? do i get to pick the order or is it timestamps
rows.expected_answer: You choose the order and the best answer is 6. Walking Ballista's 'enters with X +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect (614.1c, 614.12), and Hardened Scales and Doubling Season are further replacement effects modifying the same event. When multiple replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected permanent's controller picks which applies first (616.1), and since none of the special priorities in 616.1a-d apply, any may be chosen (616.1e). Each effect applies only once to the event (614.5). Apply Scales first (2 -> 3), then Season doubles (3 -> 6). Timestamps are irrelevant for replacement effects; that is the layer system for continuous effects.

outcome.answer: You choose the order, not timestamps. Walking Ballista's own ability that gives it counters as it enters ("This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it") counts as counters being put on it for the purposes of rule 122.6, so both **Hardened Scales** and **Doubling Season** apply as replacement effects to that event. Neither effect is a self-replacement effect, a control-changing effect, a copy effect, or a face-up/face-down effect, so per `616.1e` "any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen" by the affected object's controller (you), and you keep re-choosing until both have been applied (`616.1f`). Doubling Season's own ruling confirms replacement effects for counters stack this way, and Hardened Scales' ruling states the same for order of application: "If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects." So with X=2 you can apply them in either order: Hardened Scales first (2+1=3, then doubled = 6) or Doubling Season first (2×2=4, then +1 = 5). Since you choose, you'd pick Hardened Scales first for the better result: Walking Ballista enters with 6 +1/+1 counters.
citations: rule 616.1: "If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or t…"
rule 616.1e: "Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen."

rule 122.6: "Some spells and abilities refer to counters being put on an object. This refers to putting counters on that object while it’s on the battlefield and also to an object that’s given counters as it enter…"
oracle 4b515bb0-f275-4400-8032-3173b799ab40#0: "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it."
oracle a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6#0: "If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead."
oracle 01546b7d-a233-4176-8843-d732074dc5b6#0: "If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many of those counters on that permanent instead."

ruling a1f3da21-af6d-450e-bf0b-985d158418e6/636b245ed2960105: "If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."

rows.question: opp cast [[Blood Moon]] while i have all three tron lands out. do i still get my 7 mana from urza's? can i tap tower for 3 colorless or is it just a Mountain now
rows.expected_answer: Tron is off. Blood Moon is a type-changing effect (layer 4, 613.1d) that sets each nonbasic land's subtype to Mountain. Per 305.7, a land whose subtype is set to a basic land type loses its old land types (so it is no longer an Urza's land), loses all abilities from its rules text (the colorless mana ability), and gains only '{T}: Add {R}'. Each Urza's land is a plain Mountain that taps for one red mana; Tower does not produce three because it no longer has that ability and the others no longer have the Urza's subtype. They are still nonbasic (305.8), so Blood Moon keeps affecting them.

outcome.answer:
No — once **Blood Moon** resolves, all three Tron lands stop being Urza's Tower/Mine/Power-Plant and becomees off. Each one becomes a plain Mountain that only taps for {R}; you lose the whole Tron mana engine.

**Blood Moon** reads: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." This sets each land's subtype to Mountain, and per `305.7`, when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land "no longer has its old land type" and "loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type." That strips Urza's Tower, Urza's Mine, and Urza's Power-Plant of their land types and their `{T}: Add {C}` (plus the conditional bonus mana) abilities entirely, replacing them with just `{T}: Add {R}`, per the Scryfall ruling on Blood Moon: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'"

Since none of them are Urza's Tower/Mine/Power-Plant anymore, the "if you control..." clauses can't even check true, but it doesn't matter anyway — those abilities are gone. So no 7-mana burst, and Tower just taps for one red mana like any Mountain.
citations: rule 305.7: "the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana abil…"

ruling 94fac5fe-97d5-4c12-a80c-8efff9d853ae/de7b24c7cfc8d0d2: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability \"{T}: Add {R}.\""

rows.expected_answer: Your friend is right. Both effects are layer 4 type-changing effects (613.1d). rows.question: my goyf has two +1/+1 counters on it and I just giant growthed it. opponent [[Clone]]s it. is their clone a huge goyf too or just a regular one? and does the clone even know how big a goyf should be since the p/t is */*+1
rows.expected_answer: Just a regular Tarmogoyf. A copy acquires only the copiable values of the original (707.2): name, mana cost, types, rules text, printed P/T, etc. Counters, Giant Growth's +3/+3, and other non-copy effects are not copiable values, so the Clone gets none of them. The Clone does copy Tarmogoyf's rules text, and therefore its characteristic-defining ability (707.2a), so the Clone's own P/T is */*+1 computed from card types in graveyards (applied in layer 7a, 613.4a). The copy effect itself is applied in layer 1a (613.2a); your goyf's counters and pump are layer 7c (613.4c) and stay on your goyf only.

outcome.answer:
Just a regular Tarmogoyf — the Clone doesn't inherit the counters or the Giant Growth bonus, but it does have Tarmogoyf's power/toughness-setting ability itself, so it calculates its own size from the graveyards.

When a permanent copies another, it only takes the copiable values (name, mana cost, color, types, rules text, and printed P/T), not counters or other non-copy effects currently affecting it. Per `707.2`: "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied." Clone's own rulings confirm this directly: it "doesn't copy whether that creature is tapped or untapped, whether it has any counters on it or Auras and Equipment attached to it, or any non-copy effects that have changed its power, toughness, types, color, or so on."

However, **Tarmogoyf**'s power/toughness isn't a printed number — it's set by a characteristic-defining ability that's part of its rules text: "Tarmogoyf's power is equal to the number of card types among cards in all graveyards and its toughness is equal to that number plus 1." That ability is copied along with the rest of Tarmogoyf's text, so the Clone becomes its own Tarmogoyf that continuously calculates its own power and toughness from whatever's in the graveyards at any given time (same as the original, per the Quicksilver Gargantuan/Tarmogoyf example under `707.2`). It just doesn't start with your +1/+1 counters or your Giant Growth buff, since those are separate effects, not copiable values.
citations: rule 707.2: "Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied."

rows.question: ok classic one. I have [[Humility]] out and my opponent drops [[Opalescence]]. what are Humility and Opalescence now?? are all my creatures still 1/1? does the answer change if Opalescence was out first?
rows.expected_answer: Walk the layers. Opalescence reads 'each OTHER non-Aura enchantment', so it never affects itself: Opalescence stays a noncreature enchantment and keeps its ability in every scenario. Layer 4 (613.1d): Opalescence makes Humility a 'creature' enchantment. Layer 6 (613.1f): Humility removes all abilities from every creature, including itself; per 613.6 an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers even though its source ability is gone. Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility's 'base P/T 1/1' and Opalescence's 'base P/T equal to mana value' both set Humility's P/T. Neither depends on the other under 613.8a (applying one doesn't change the text, existence, or targets of the other), so timestamp order decides (613.7). If Opalescence has the later timestamp: Humility is a 4/4 creature with no abilities. If Humility has the later timestamp: Humility is a 1/1 creature with no abilities. Either way every ordinary creature is a 1/1 with no abilities, and Opalescence is an unaffected noncreature enchantment. Any other non-Aura enchantment Opalescence animates follows Humility itself: its base power and toughness are its mana value when Opalescence is later, and 1/1 when Humility is.

rows.question: quick one: if I have [[Valki, God of Lies]] in hand can I just cast the Tibalt side for 7? and while it's in my library/graveyard does it count as a planeswalker card for stuff like Vraska's Contempt / Kaya's Ghostform?
rows.expected_answer: Yes. Valki // Tibalt is a modal double-faced card: when you cast it you choose which face you're casting before it goes on the stack, and only that face is evaluated (712.11b, 712.11c), so you can cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for {5}{B}{R} straight from your hand. Once chosen, the spell/permanent has only that face's characteristics (712.8f). But anywhere other than the stack or battlefield (hand, library, graveyard, exile) an MDFC has only its front face's characteristics (712.8a), so it is a legendary creature card named Valki, God of Lies there — never a planeswalker card.

outcome.answer:
Yes and no. **Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor** is a modal double-faced card, so under `712.11b` you choose which face to cast before it hits the stack, and you can cast the Tibalt side by paying its own cost, {5}{B}{R} (7 mana). While it's on the stack or on the battlefield as Tibalt, `712.8f` says it "has only the characteristics of the face that's up," so it's a Legendary Planeswalker there — Vraska's Contempt can target it, and Kaya's Ghostform on it would be enchanting a planeswalker.

But once it leaves the battlefield or stack — to graveyard, exile, or library — `712.8a` takes over: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face." The front face is Valki, a Legendary Creature, not a planeswalker. So sitting in your library or graveyard, the card is a creature card, not a planeswalker card, no matter which face it was cast or died as. Kaya's Ghostform's own ability doesn't care about card type (it just returns "that card"), but any effect that specifically checks whether the card in a hidden/graveyard zone is a planeswalker card would only see it as a creature card there.
citations: rule 712.11b: "A player casting a modal double-faced card or a copy of a modal double-faced card as a spell chooses which face they are casting before putting it onto the stack."
rule 712.8f: "While a modal double-faced spell is on the stack or a modal double-faced permanent is on the battlefield, it has only the characteristics of the face that’s up."
rule 712.8a: "While a double-faced card is outside the game or in a zone other than the battlefield or stack, it has only the characteristics of its front face."

rows.question: cast Stomp off my bonecrusher giant, it resolved and went to exile. my opp says I can only cast the creature half from exile now, not Stomp again, is that right? also can they counter Stomp with a 'counter target creature spell' effect since the card is a creature?
rows.expected_answer: Your opponent is right. When an Adventure spell resolves it is exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and you may cast the card from exile — but only as the creature (Bonecrusher Giant), not as Stomp again (715.3d). And no, Stomp can't be hit by 'counter target creature spell': while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only its alternative characteristics (715.3a, 715.3b), so it is a red instant, not a creature spell. Everywhere else, including exile, the card is just the creature card Bonecrusher Giant (715.4).

outcome.answer:
Your opponent is right on both counts. When you cast **Bonecrusher Giant // Stomp** as the Adventure, the spell on the stack only has Stomp's alternative characteristics (`715.3b`: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."), so it's an Instant, not a Creature spell — a 'counter target creature spell' effect simply can't target it, since it isn't a creature spell at that time.

Once Stomp resolves, its controller exiles it instead of putting it in the graveyard, per `715.3d`: "Instead of putting a spell that was cast as an Adventure into its owner's graveyard as it resolves, its controller exiles it. For as long as that card remains exiled, that player may play it. It can't be cast as an Adventure this way." So from exile you can only cast Bonecrusher Giant as the creature — you can't cast Stomp again from there.
citations: rule 715.3b: "While on the stack as an Adventure, the spell has only its alternative characteristics."

rows.question: melded my Bruna and Gisela into Brisela and then it got Path to Exiled. does that count as one creature leaving or two for my [[Blood Artist]] type triggers, and do I get one Plains or two off Path?
rows.expected_answer:
Blood Artist does not trigger at all here: Path to Exile exiles Brisela, and Blood Artist
triggers on a creature dying, which means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield
(700.4). Exile is not dying. If Brisela instead died (say, to a Wrath of God), Blood Artist
would trigger exactly once: one permanent left the battlefield, even though the melded
permanent is a single object represented by two cards (712.21, 701.42a). A trigger reading
"whenever a card is put into a graveyard" would see two cards (712.21e). Either way, the
search happens once and Bruna and Gisela both go to exile. It is Brisela's controller who
searches, not the player who cast Path to Exile ("Its controller may search their library
for a basic land card"), and any basic land will do, not only a Plains.

outcome.answer:
Neither trigger fires the way you'd expect, and here's why: Path to Exile doesn't kill Brisela, so **Blood Artist** never sees a death at all. Path to Exile's Oracle text is "Exile target creature," not "destroy" — and Blood Artist only triggers when a creature "dies," which specifically means being put into a graveyard from the battlefield. Exiling Brisela sends her (well, both her component cards) to exile, not the graveyard, so it's not a death and Blood Artist doesn't trigger at all, not once and not twice.

As for the land: Path to Exile only nets you **one** basic land, not two. Even though a melded permanent leaving the battlefield puts two cards into the new zone (`712.21`: "one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone"), the melded permanent still only counts as **one object** for purposes of any effect that cares about how many things changed zones (`712.21e`: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved"). Path to Exile's ability triggers off exiling one target creature and lets its controller search for "a basic land card" (singular) — one instance of the ability, one search, one land, tapped, then shuffle if you searched.

So net result: no Blood Artist trigger, and one basic land (e.g. one Plains) if you choose to search.
citations: oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."
oracle d683d985-9888-4d21-8b5f-69e69ce4a03b#0: "Exile target creature. Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle."
rule 712.21: "If a melded permanent leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves the battlefield and two cards are put into the appropriate zone."
rule 712.21e: "If an effect needs to know the number of objects that changed zones, a melded permanent among those objects counts as one object that moved."

rows.question: old school question. my Waylay (Urza's Saga printing) says 'at end of turn, remove them from the game'. so I cast it during my opponent's end step, the knights survive since the end step already started, and I get to swing with them on my turn right? classic waylay trick
rows.expected_answer: No — that trick was closed by errata. The printed text is not what the card does; you always use the current Oracle wording (108.1), which is 'Create three 2/2 white Knight creature tokens. Exile them at the beginning of the next cleanup step.' If you cast Waylay in your opponent's end step, the Knights are exiled at that same turn's cleanup step: the game checks for triggered abilities waiting during cleanup, puts the 'beginning of the next cleanup step' trigger on the stack, and then players get priority and another cleanup step follows (514.3a). You never get to attack with them. (Casting it during your opponent's declare-attackers step to get surprise blockers still works.)

rows.question: my mirage LED says 'play this ability as an interrupt'. so it's a mana ability and I can crack it in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to pay for it right? that way I still have tutor as the last card when I discard
rows.expected_answer: No. Ignore the printed 'interrupt' text and use the current Oracle wording (108.1): 'Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant.' It is still a mana ability — the timing restriction doesn't change that (605.1) — but 'Activate only as an instant' means you may only activate it when you have priority (602.5e), so you can't activate it while paying for a spell the way 605.3a normally allows for mana abilities. The correct play is to cast Infernal Tutor with Tutor as the last card in hand, hold priority, then activate LED in response; when Tutor resolves you are hellbent and the mana is still floating.

outcome.answer:
First, note your Mirage copy is outdated: current Oracle text for **Lion's Eye Diamond** is "Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color. Activate only as an instant." (the old "play as an interrupt" wording no longer applies).

No, you can't crack LED in the middle of casting Infernal Tutor to help pay for it. LED is a mana ability, but its "Activate only as an instant" clause means you can only activate it when you actually have priority and could cast an instant (`602.5e`: "the player must follow the timing rules for casting an instant spell"). While you're in the middle of casting a spell (announcing it, locking in costs, paying costs), you don't have priority — that's a fixed sequence of steps, not a priority window — so LED can't be squeezed in there, confirmed by Scryfall's own ruling that "it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant."

The good news is you don't need to force it in there anyway. As soon as you cast Infernal Tutor, it leaves your hand and moves to the stack (`601.2a`: "a player first moves that card...from where it is to the stack"). So pay Infernal Tutor's {1}{B} cost with normal mana, finish casting it, then (now that you have priority again) activate LED in response if you want its mana for something else. At that point Infernal Tutor is already on the stack, not in your hand, so cracking LED afterward won't discard it — you just can't use LED's own mana to fund Tutor's cast.

rule 602.5e: "the player must follow the timing rules for casting an instant spell, though the ability isn’t actually an instant."
rule 601.2a: "a player first moves that card (or that copy of a card) from where it is to the stack."
ruling ee6099b0-fb1f-42f1-b862-7708c6e36d05/311e9a5aa9d6c7d6: "it can only be activated at times when you can cast an instant."

rows.question: ok so I have [[Blood Artist]] out and my opponent wraths with [[Wrath of God]]. Blood Artist dies at the same time as everything else so does it even see the other creatures die? do I drain for all of them or just itself?
rows.expected_answer: Yes, you drain for every creature that died, including Blood Artist itself. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities 'look back in time' (603.10, 603.6c): the game checks the state immediately before the event, when Blood Artist was still on the battlefield, so it sees every creature that died simultaneously, including itself. All those triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (603.3), and you choose a target player for each one.

outcome.answer: Yes, it drains for all of them, including itself. **Blood Artist**'s trigger is "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life," which is a leaves-the-battlefield ability, and those abilities "look back in time" per `603.10a` to see the game state immediately before the event. So even though Blood Artist and the rest of your board die simultaneously to **Wrath of God**, the game checks the board as it existed right before the destruction to see what died, and Blood Artist's ability triggers once for itself and once for every other creature that died in that wrath. Scryfall's own ruling on Blood Artist confirms this directly: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures." Each trigger is a separate instance of the ability, each draining 1 life, so you end up gaining life and draining life equal to the total number of creatures that died (Blood Artist plus every other creature Wrath of God killed).
citations: rule 603.10a: "Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities, abilities that trigger when a player sacrifices a permanent, abilities that trigger when a card leaves a gravey…"
ruling 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d/eaf0e0e76c3621ab: "If Blood Artist and one or more other creatures die at the same time, its ability will trigger for each of those creatures."
oracle 310f141c-7f37-4729-aed6-dd9c09db448d#0: "Whenever this creature or another creature dies, target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life."

rows.question: my buddy says once I cast a spell he can't respond until I 'pass'. I cast Lightning Bolt at his bob, do I get to keep going and cast a second Bolt before he gets a chance to counter the first one?
rows.expected_answer: Your buddy is half right. After you cast a spell you receive priority again (117.3c), so you may cast the second Bolt immediately, before he can respond to the first. He only gets priority when you pass. Nothing resolves until all players pass in succession with the stack non-empty (117.4); then only the top object resolves, and the active player gets priority again after it resolves (117.3b). So he can still respond to either Bolt once you pass, but you are entitled to stack both first.

rows.question: I control a 2/2 with a Giant Growth resolving on it, and mid-resolution of a different spell it's technically at 0 toughness for a second (Maro-style hand-size thing). Does it die? And separately, if I have two Ragavan on the battlefield somehow, when exactly does the legend rule kick in - can I respond in between?
rows.expected_answer: 1) It doesn't die. State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, not in the middle of a spell resolving (704.3, 704.4 - the CR's own Maro example). The creature only dies if it still has toughness 0 or less when SBAs are next checked (704.5f). 2) The legend rule (704.5j) is also a state-based action: the moment a player would get priority with two Ragavans you control, you choose one and the other goes to the graveyard. It doesn't use the stack and there is no window to respond between the second Ragavan entering and the legend rule applying; you can only respond before the second one enters/resolves.

rows.question: I attack with a 5/5 trample that also has deathtouch (Questing Beast) and they block with a 4/4. how much can I trample over? my opponent says I have to assign 4 to the blocker first
rows.expected_answer: The premise is off: Questing Beast is a 4/4 with vigilance, deathtouch and haste, and it does not have trample, so blocked by one creature it assigns all its combat damage to that blocker and nothing goes to the player (510.1c). A good answer says so. For the creature the asker describes, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 and can trample 4 over to the player. Trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blockers before excess goes to the player (702.19b), but any nonzero damage from a deathtouch source counts as lethal for that purpose (702.2c). Damage assignment for a blocked creature follows 510.1c, then all combat damage is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between (510.2). The 4/4 is then destroyed by deathtouch as an SBA.

outcome.answer:
First, a correction: Questing Beast's actual Oracle text is "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste... Questing Beast can't be blocked by creatures with power 2 or less... Combat damage that would be dealt by creatures you control can't be prevented... Whenever Questing Beast deals combat damage to an opponent, it deals that much damage to target planeswalker that player controls." It does not have trample at all, so unless something else is granting it trample, none of its damage tramples through — it's blocked, so it assigns all its combat damage to the blocking creature per 510.1c, and none to the player.

If you *do* have a source granting Questing Beast trample, your opponent is still wrong. Because Questing Beast has deathtouch, you don't need to assign 4 damage (the blocker's toughness) to make it "lethal." Per `702.2c`, "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt," and per `702.19b`, once lethal damage is assigned to the blocker, the rest can go to the player. So with trample and deathtouch, you'd only need to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 blocker and could send the remaining 4 damage (or however much your creature deals) trampling over to the player.
citations: oracle b685757b-521e-4353-a233-97052359723d#0: "Vigilance, deathtouch, haste"

rows.question: commander q: my commander is [[Kenrith, the Returned King]]. two things: 1) can I run Nicol Bolas, the Ravager since Kenrith's text mentions all 5 colors? and 2) someone bounced Kenrith to my hand with Unsummon - does he go to the command zone or is that only for graveyard/exile?
rows.expected_answer: 1) Yes. Color identity includes mana symbols in the mana cost AND in the rules text (903.4), so Kenrith's identity is WUBRG even though his mana cost is only {4}{W}. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager (UBR) is legal because every color in its identity is in Kenrith's (903.5c). 2) Yes, Kenrith can go to the command zone. If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead - a replacement effect (903.9b). Graveyard/exile use a separate state-based action (903.9a). Either way it's optional.

outcome.answer:
Two separate answers here.

1) Yes. **Kenrith, the Returned King**'s activated ability costs use every color of mana ({R}, {1}{G}, {2}{W}, {3}{U}, {4}{B}), and color identity is defined by "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text" (`903.4`). Since those symbols appear in Kenrith's rules text, his color identity is all five colors (WUBRG). A card can go in your deck "only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck's commander" (`903.5c`), and **Nicol Bolas, the Ravager**'s color identity (blue/black/red) is entirely covered by Kenrith's five-color identity, so Bolas is legal to include.

2) He may go to the command zone, at your choice, not automatically to hand. Rule `903.9b` states: "If a commander would be put into its owner's hand or library from anywhere, its owner may put it into the command zone instead. This replacement effect may apply more than once to the same event." So when **Unsummon** returns Kenrith to your hand, you as his owner may choose to redirect that into the command zone instead — it's optional, and if you decline he simply goes to your hand as normal.

rows.question: commander damage question. I've been hit for 15 by my opponent's Rafiq. she then copies it with a Clone and hits me for 6 more with the clone. do I lose? also does the 21 count noncombat damage like from Fling?
rows.expected_answer: No to both. A player loses when they've been dealt 21 or more COMBAT damage by the SAME commander over the course of the game (903.10a; checked as a state-based action, 704.6c). The Clone copying Rafiq is not a commander, so its 6 damage isn't commander damage - you're still at 15 from the real Rafiq. Fling damage is noncombat, so it never counts toward the 21 either; it just reduces your life total normally.

outcome.answer:
You do not lose from commander damage on this line — and no, Fling-style noncombat damage never counts toward the 21 either. Two separate points here.

First, the special commander-damage loss condition only counts damage from the actual card designated as your commander, not from anything else that merely copies it. Per `903.10a`, "A player who's been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game." A Clone that copies **Rafiq of the Many** becomes a creature with Rafiq's copiable characteristics, but it is not itself the commander — the commander designation is an attribute of the specific card, not something a copy effect grants. As the rules note under `903.3` explains, "A permanent that's copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player's graveyard) is not a commander." So the 15 combat damage from the real Rafiq and the 6 combat damage from the Clone don't add together for the 21-damage-from-the-same-commander check; you'd need 21 from the actual Rafiq permanent itself. You still lost 21 life total overall, but the special SBA loss condition in `903.10a` isn't triggered by this combination.

Second, that same rule text specifies "combat damage" only. Damage from **Fling** — even if you sacrificed the actual commander creature to cast it — is not combat damage, so it never contributes to the 21 needed for the commander-damage loss condition, regardless of source. It just reduces your life total normally.
citations: rule 903.10a: "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game."
rule 903.3: "A permanent that’s copying a commander (such as a Body Double, for example, copying a commander in a player’s graveyard) is not a commander."
rule 903.3: "This designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself."

rows.question: two quick ones. 1) if I tap all my lands during my upkeep does that mana stick around so I can cast the mind sculptor in my main phase? 2) when I'm casting snappy can I tap lands in the middle of casting it or do I have to float the mana first?
rows.expected_answer: 1) No. Each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, so mana added during your upkeep is lost before your main phase (106.4). Tap the lands in your main phase instead. 2) Yes. Casting a spell includes a step where, if the total cost includes mana, you get a chance to activate mana abilities such as tapping lands (601.2g), and only then do you pay the total cost (601.2h). You do not need to float mana before announcing the spell.

outcome.answer:
1) No. Mana empties from your pool at the end of each step and phase (this is a core game rule, though the exact text wasn't in the material I have to quote), so any mana you produce during your upkeep is gone before you reach your main phase. You'll need to tap your lands again in the main phase to cast **Jace, the Mind Sculptor**.

2) You don't need to float mana beforehand. Casting a spell is a single process: you announce the spell and its costs/targets, the total cost gets "locked in" per `601.2f`, and only then do you get a window to activate mana abilities — per `601.2g`, "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities... Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid." You then actually pay the cost per `601.2h`, "The player pays the total cost. First, they pay all costs that don't involve random elements or moving objects from the library to a public zone, in any order." So while casting **Snapcaster Mage** you can tap your lands for mana right in the middle of the casting process, after announcing it and before paying — there's no need to have mana already floating.
citations: rule 601.2g: "If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid."
rule 601.2f: "Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes “locked in.”"
rule 601.2h: "The player pays the total cost. First, they pay all costs that don’t involve random elements or moving objects from the library to a public zone, in any order."

rows.question: my opp has [[bob]] and flipped a tim off the top, then next turn he flipped a goyf. how much life does he lose each time? goyf is like a 5/6 rn so is it 5?
rows.expected_answer: Dark Confidant makes you lose life equal to the revealed card's mana value, which is the total mana in its mana cost regardless of color (202.3). Prodigal Sorcerer costs {2}{U}, so he loses 3 life. Tarmogoyf costs {1}{G}, so he loses 2 life. Tarmogoyf's power/toughness is irrelevant; mana value is based only on the mana cost.

outcome.answer:
For **Dark Confidant**, life loss is always based on the mana value of the card, never on its printed power/toughness, current stats, or nickname. Its ability reads: "You lose life equal to its mana value," and mana value is defined as "a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color" (`202.3`).

So for the Tarmogoyf flip: even though it might currently be a 5/6 (its power/toughness comes from a characteristic-defining ability, not its cost), that has zero effect on the life loss. Tarmogoyf's mana cost is {1}{G}, so its mana value is 2 — your opponent loses 2 life for that flip, not 5.

As for "Tim," I don't have that card's actual name or mana cost in front of me, so I can't give you an exact number for it — but the same rule applies: whatever its printed mana cost is (with X treated as 0 per the ruling below if it has one), that's the life total lost, regardless of what the card does or how it's nicknamed. If you tell me the actual card, I can nail down the exact number.
citations: rule 202.3: "The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color."
